annotations.annotation_text: HCE manifestation "Earwicker" on page 73 within "The Trial of HCE": here the universal father-figure Humphrey Chimpden Earwicker appears in the context of the public trial and persecution of HCE, the ballad of Hosty, and the testimony of witnesses. During this Age of Gods phase, HCE embodies the patriarch whose guilt, grandeur, and fall drive the cyclical dream forward.
sources: Glasheen, Adaline. Third Census of Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/thirdcensusoffin0000glas
McHugh, Roland. The Sigla of Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/siglaoffinnegans0000mchu
James Joyce Digital Archive: Finnegans Wake Notons. https://jjda.ie

annotations.annotation_text: Tavern/jury motif "Bar" on page 73 ("The Trial of HCE"): the twelve customers drinking in HCE's Chapelizod pub represent public opinion, the Zodiac, and the Apostles within the public trial and persecution of HCE, the ballad of Hosty, and the testimony of witnesses. During this Age of Gods phase, they judge, condemn, and demand another round — the Greek chorus of middle-class Dublin gossip.
sources: Glasheen, Adaline. Third Census of Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/thirdcensusoffin0000glas
Campbell, Joseph and Robinson, Henry Morton. A Skeleton Key. https://archive.org/details/skeletonkeytofin00camp
Gordon, John. Finnegans Blog (Tavern chapters). https://johngordonfinnegan.weebly.com

annotations.annotation_text: Dublin landmark "Howth" on page 73 ("The Trial of HCE"): grounding the cosmic dream in physical Dublin during the public trial and persecution of HCE, the ballad of Hosty, and the testimony of witnesses. Joyce transforms this real location into a universal archetypal site — simultaneously Eden, Waterloo, Calvary, and the Elysian Fields — within the Age of Gods phase.
sources: Joyce, P.W. The Origin and History of Irish Names of Places. https://archive.org/details/originandhistory01joycuoft
Mink, Louis O. A Finnegans Wake Gazetteer. https://archive.org/details/finneganswakegaz0000mink
